label: text
text: Gruesome" Exhibits In Court.

label: text
text: A DAGGER MARK?

label: text
text: Shoulder Bone Shown to

label: text
text: Cross-examination as the resumed hearing to-day of the Western Market alleged murder case centred round a depression in a shoulder bone of the deceased.

label: text
text: The bone in question, with two others, was produced in court by Dr. E. P. Minett, Government, bacteriologist, who had detached them from the body subsequent to an exhumation carried out on Tuesday.

label: text
text: Dr. Minett, in evidence, stated that the body was in an advanced state of decomposition when exhumed and recognition by features was impossible. The bones were imbedded in a semi-tibial mass of decomposed material and appeared to be those of an adult male.

label: text
text: The body had been identified, said Dr. Minett, by the string used in the mortary for sowing up bodies and witness had then proceeded to detach the three bones in question. In the large bone of the upper (left) arm there was an depression measuring half an inch long, 3/8 of an inch across at its widest part and about the same measurement in depth. The soft inner part of the bone was exposed.

label: text
text: Mr. A. Dyer Ball (for the Crown): Do you connect that in any way with the dagger found on the accused?

label: text
text: Dr. Minett: It might have been caused by a weapon similar to the dagger.

label: text
text: Asked if he had anything in his mind as to the situation now of the dagger in question. Dr. Minett said that his impression was that if the depression in the bone was caused by the striking of a dagger," he would have expected the depression in the bone to be cleaner, to have smoother edges, if the point of the dagger had not been turned.

label: text
text: Asked if a point of a dagger would be turned by meeting a bone, Dr. Minet said he thought it would have to be very soft metal.

label: text
text: In reply to other questions, witness said that the wound in question could have been caused by the dagger in its present-turned state.

label: text
text: Cross-examined by Mr. H. S. Fitzroy (for the defence) witness said that he did not know anything about steel.

label: text
text: Mr. Fitzroy: Could the depression have been caused by an instrument with a sharp point?

label: text
text: Mr. Fitzroy: "Can you say if it is possible for the infliction of a severe wound on the shoulder blade, such as the prisoner bears marks of, to cause loss of memory?

label: text
text: Witness (after examining the large scar on the prisoner's shoulder): I cannot say. It might or it might not.

label: text
text: Witness added that the scar stopped short an inch and a half from the spinal column.

label: text
text: The examination of further witnesses is proceeding.

label: text
text: In view of suggestions both in Hong Kong and Shanghai that armed expeditions be sent by the Clinton Government to stamp out piracy, it is interesting to note that a brigade of Nationalist troops have again been to the fore in an intensive campaign against outlaws.

[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Päkkik. Konmoons Nov. 23.

label: text
text: Brigadier Chu King-tong of the 60th Brigade has won further laurels in his efforts against bandits.

label: text
text: Recently I reported his transfer from this district to Heungshan where he also did good work. On his coming back, he immediately told his men to Lai'Ngok, which has an area of about 50 square lias and comprises about 20 villages.

label: text
text: [Note: a life is Chinese linear measurement, equal to "about a third of a mile".]

label: text
text:
By reason of its proximity to Kongmoon proper, Lai Ngok has been a terror for law-abiding people.
Nearly all the inhabitants are pirates, kinsfolk of pirates, receivers, or are otherwise associated with the nefarious calling.
It was the first time that the den was broken into.

label: text
text: Brizadier Chu was accompanied by his Russian adviser, who recently arrived from Canton. Both went into action.

label: text
text:
Stubborn resistance was offered. Snipers hiding in the fields, or pretending to be farmers, picked off the advancing soldierry, who suffered over twenty casualties in the fray.
Anybody unable to prove his or her bona fides was summarily dethoth with. Houses were set afire in rows, and the work of devastation was done so completely that every one of the Lai Ngok community fled.
After that a systematic search was made and steps taken to prevent the pitates and their relatives getting back.

label: text
text: News of the successful repulse of an attempted piratien attack in the West River yesterday had reached the Colony by wireless from the armed launch which beat off the pirates.

label: text
text:
It appears that the tow-launch "Mun. Tong," together with two lighters bearing a cargo of wood, was on the way to Hong Kong from Wuchow when "pirates opened fire near Kubo and called on the vessels to stop."
"The armed convoy launch, one of the many which are engaged" on anti-piracy work in accompanying "tows" and doing patrol work, replied to the fire very effectively and the pirates decamped.

label: paragraph_title
text: "One Man Wounded"

label: text
text: The wireless message states that "one man on board was wounded and sent to 'Kongmoon.' It is not stated whether the man was a member of the Chinese crew but it is presumed that this must be the case.

label: text
text: The “Mun Tong” is due to arrive in Hong Kong later in the day.

label: paragraph_title
text: Mutilation of Names &

label: text
text: السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته

label: text
text: Local shipping circles had another "piracy" scare this morning through mutilation in translation of names and places.

label: text
text: This report, which had come by way of Canton, concerned the French conster “Hanoi” the report of which was published on Nov. 13.

label: text
text:
It appears that the news got back to Kwong-chow-wan (the French colony in Kwangtung) and then spread to Canton.
Confusion was increased by the mention of there being $50,000 in treasure on board this French boat which "piled between Hong Kong, Saigon and Bangkok."

label: text
text: As a matter of fact, the "Hanol" had $5,000 on board, consigned by the Chinese Maritime Customs at Pakhoi for deposit with the Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank here.

label: paragraph_title

Questions in House of

label: text
text: WHO IS TO BLAME.

label: text
text: Chinese Government Not Implicated.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, when questions were being answered, after Sir Austen Chamberlain, the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, had given an account of the attack on the steamer "Sunning" on November 15, Capt. J. G. Fairfax asked whether these incidents were not becoming increasingly frequent and whether the attack was by pirates or under any organised Chinese authority.

label: text
text: Sir Austen Chamberlain agreed that acts of piracy were unhappy frequent.

label: text
text: He declared this was undoubtedly an act of piracy by pirates, and should not be confused with any action of the Chinese Government. —Reuter.

label: text
text:
Joint Action by the Powers?
London, Nov. 24.

label: text
text: The "Daily Telegraph's" Washington correspondent states that following the report of the American delegates to the conference on the revision of the Chinese customstariff, and abolition of extraterritoriality, it is believed likely that President Coolidge will initiate consideration by the Powers of steps to end the state of anarchy in China.

label: text
text: Mr. Coolidge is known to be opposed to the United States joining the armed intervention enterprise, but that change is mind if the American Legation or American nationals are gravely imperilled.—Reuter.

STRANGE IDENTITY
PARADE.

label: text
text: LUKONG CHARGED.

label: text
text:
"It is a case of somebody else's papers found in somebody else's bed and being hidden by somebody else," said Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., at the Central Magistracy this morning, when defending a Cantonese lukong charged with unlawfully receiving $6.50 from passengers arriving in the Colony on board the s.s. "Tung On" on November 7.
The case, which had been before Mr. R. E. Lindsell on several previous occasions, had been adjourned on Monday last when Captain H. F. Bloxham, A.S.P., closed the case for the prosecution.

label: text
text: At the commencement of this morning's proceedings, Mr. Alabaster, who appeared upon instructions from Mr. Leo d'Almada, said that he understood that His Worship had hinted that he might allow the prosecution to re-open their case. Should that be so, he, Mr. Alabaster, would argue that the learned magistrate had no power to do so.

label: text
text: Mr. Lindsell said that he might permit evidence as to the authority of the defendant as a police officer to accept any money. As a matter of fact, since the last hearing he had decided to make a slight amendment to the charge and that would not necessitate reopening the case.

label: paragraph_title
text: Parade a Farce

label: text
text: Mr. Alabaster said that he would make a few comments before putting the defendant in the box. The charge was a nebulous one, the papers were not found in the defendant's bed, but in a bed belonging to somebody else,—a man whose number had been given but who had not been called. There was good reason to believe that this was a case of mis-taken identity. In his counsel's

Balksi, Koramoon, Nov. 23

label: text
text: The proprietors of the Kam Ling Hotel (West Point) were summoned before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning for obstruction. Mr. W. B. Hind, defending, urged that the offence was purely a technical one and asked for a nominal fine. The Magistrate said that he agreed with counsel and would impose a fine of $3 only.

label: paragraph_title
text: Unworthy of Credit!

label: text
text: Counsel submitted that the evidence was wholly unworthy of credit and asked the Magistrate to dismiss the charge.

label: text
text: His Worship held that the prosecution had brought forward sufficient evidence to lead a jury to believe that the money was paid as a gratuity and rejected counsel's application.

label: text
text: Defendant in the witness box said that he had been in the Police Force for five years. Witness outlined his movements on the day of the alleged offence and denied having had any communication with a former witness and also having called at the boarding house where the offence was alleged to have been committed. At this stage the case was adjourned until 9.30 this afternoon.

label: text
text: Over 2,000,000 Tons a Week.

label: text
text: RESTRICTIONS RELAXED.

label: text

South Wales and Northumberland
Obdurate.

label: text
text: Colonel Lane Fox, Secretary for Mines, announced in the House of Commons to-day a relaxation of the coal restrictions. Although supplies were still far short of the normal demands, the output, he said, was steadily increasing, and the time had come when practically all restrictions except that which prohibited the export of coal ought to be withdrawn and freedom re-

label: text
text: The restrictions on gas and electricity for light and heating power would be withdrawn as from tomorrow. The restrictions on the domestic consumption of coal would be continued only to the end of the present week.

label: text
text: As from tomorrow, also, the colonies would be given freedom to dispose of coal as they pleased in this country.

label: text
text: Some 10,976 more miners are at work to-day, bringing the total up to 421,478.—British Wireless Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Die-Hards

label: text
text: London: Nov. 24.

label: text
text: The South Wales and Northumberland, Durham and Cumberland are proving the two most die-hard coalfields in the matter of the settlement.

label: text
text: While agreement is under way in most of the other districts, the Northumberland miners' group has rejected the owners' tentative terms. A complete deadlock has been reached in South Wales.

label: text
text: It is noteworthy that these are not only the largest colliery groups, but show the lowest proportion of defections.

label: text
text: Production Rapidly Increasing. London Nov. 24.

label: text
text: That the rapidly increasing production of coal is now over 2,000,000 tons a week was mentioned by Colonel Lane Fox in the House of Commons when announcing that practically all restrictions on the movements and employment of coal were being withdrawn almost immediately, except those governing export.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: Rugby, Nov. 24.

label: text
text:
The miners returning to the pits yesterday numbered 20,121, the largest increase since the stoppage began, thus bringing the total engaged at the pits to 400,500. Good progress was made yesterday in the district negotiations between local leaders and colliery proprietors, and provisional agreements have been reached in several coalfields.
Relaxation of coal restrictions, with particular reference to fuel industries, will be announced in the House of Commons to-day.—British Wireless Service.
